global.h3: US holds fire on Iran as Hormuz deal takes shape
global.summary: Washington says it is locked and loaded but agreed to pause strikes while a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and cap Iran's nuclear program is negotiated.
body: President Trump said the United States was ready to move against Iran but held off after Tehran and several Gulf states asked for time to finalise the outline of an agreement. The framework would reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping and put an end to what Washington calls Iran's nuclear threat.

No US strikes inside Iran have been reported for several days after what the president described as a heavy wave of attacks the previous week. Trump said talks with Iran would begin Monday to lock the terms in place, while Gulf capitals push for a durable ceasefire rather than another pause.

global.h3: Hormuz shipping crisis chokes tanker traffic
global.summary: Repeated Iranian attacks on vessels and a US naval response have turned the world's most important oil chokepoint into a war zone.
body: The standoff traces back to a June memorandum meant to end the Iran war. Since then Iran has repeatedly threatened and attacked ships in the Strait of Hormuz, trying to force vessels to follow routes and pay fees set by Tehran.

Attacks on three ships on July 6 and 7 prompted US strikes and led Trump to declare the earlier truce over. A US naval presence now shadows the strait as insurers and shippers reroute around the risk.

global.h3: Gaza truce push wobbles as Israel keeps striking
global.summary: Israeli strikes left a crater at a Gaza hospital days after Trump announced Hamas and Israel had agreed to advance a ceasefire plan.
body: A Board of Peace official called it a tense moment as Israel continued lethal airstrikes in Gaza, even after the US president said the two sides had agreed to move a ceasefire plan forward. Senior Israeli officials stressed they had not agreed to suspend operations against Hamas.

The gap between the diplomatic announcement and events on the ground has raised doubts about how binding the framework really is, with mediators warning that renewed strikes could collapse the process.

global.h3: Israeli defence minister and IDF clash over West Bank general
global.summary: The defence minister announced he was replacing the top general in the West Bank, and the military promptly said he could not.
body: The Times of Israel reported a sharp institutional clash after the defence minister moved to replace the senior commander in the West Bank. The IDF pushed back publicly, saying the minister lacked the authority to make the change.
The dispute exposes friction inside Israel's security establishment at a moment when the government is juggling Gaza, tensions with Iran and unrest in the occupied territories.

global.h3: Russian missiles pound Kyiv as US steps back from NATO role
global.summary: Deadly overnight strikes hit the Ukrainian capital while Washington signals it will hand off its lead role coordinating NATO support for Kyiv.
body: Russia opened August with a fresh wave of missiles and drones on Kyiv, killing residents and wounding others. President Zelenskyy said a shortage of Patriot interceptors was emboldening Moscow to keep hitting cities.
The mood darkened after signals that the Pentagon intends to step back from its lead role coordinating NATO military support, leaving European capitals to shoulder more of the burden.

global.h3: Ukraine drones hit 13 Russian energy sites
global.summary: Kyiv answered with long-range strikes on Russian energy infrastructure and reported sinking a Russian ship.
body: Ukrainian forces struck at least 13 energy facilities inside Russia and occupied territory, causing blackouts affecting Russian troop positions. Kyiv also reported strikes in Crimea and the Kherson region and said it had sunk a Russian vessel.
One person was killed and several hurt when a Russian guided bomb struck Zaporizhzhia, and a college in Odesa was reported hit, keeping civilian casualties high on both sides.

global.h3: Saudi crown prince warns Trump on new Iran strikes
global.summary: Riyadh urged caution as Washington weighed whether to resume attacks, fearing a wider Gulf war.
body: Trump spoke by phone with the Saudi crown prince, who raised concerns about potential fresh US attacks on Iran and the risk to Gulf stability and energy exports.
Gulf states have pressed both Washington and Tehran to convert the current pause into a lasting settlement, wary that another escalation would put their own infrastructure in the firing line.

global.h3: Oil markets swing on Hormuz risk
global.summary: Crude and shipping costs stayed volatile as traders priced the chance of the strait closing outright.
body: With roughly a fifth of the world's oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz, the on-again off-again US-Iran confrontation has kept crude prices and tanker insurance rates elevated.
Analysts warn that a full closure, even briefly, would send energy prices sharply higher and ripple through inflation figures in import-dependent economies across Europe and Asia.

global.h3: European drought threatens Dutch dikes and German river trade
global.summary: A run of dry, hot summers is drying out peat dikes in the Netherlands and dropping river levels that carry German cargo.
body: Inland dikes near Waddinxveen are built of peat that must stay damp to hold back water, and the prolonged drought is weakening them. Water managers are watching vulnerable stretches closely as the dry spell drags on.
Falling levels on the Rhine and connected waterways are also squeezing German barge trade, forcing shippers to lighten loads and raising costs across an economy that leans heavily on river freight.

global.h3: Fourth heatwave of the year bakes western Europe
global.summary: Tropical temperatures returned across the Low Countries and neighbouring regions as August began hot and dry.
body: Forecasters recorded a fourth heatwave of the year in the southern Netherlands, with August starting under abundant sunshine and temperatures in the low thirties. Similar conditions stretched across parts of western Europe.
The heat is compounding the drought, stressing crops, waterways and power and water systems, and keeping climate adaptation squarely in the public conversation.

netherlands.h3: Drought puts Dutch water defences on watch
netherlands.summary: The deepening dry spell is weakening peat dikes and lowering rivers, a slow-burning stress test for the country's water management.
body: The Netherlands prides itself on flood control, but this summer the threat is running the other way. A prolonged drought is drying out inland peat dikes that need moisture to stay strong, and water authorities are monitoring at-risk sections around Waddinxveen and beyond.

Low river levels are also hurting freight on the Rhine, a reminder that the same climate pressures reshaping winters are now testing Dutch summers. Officials are weighing water-use restrictions if conditions worsen.

netherlands.h3: PRO opens poll lead as progressives desert D66
netherlands.summary: Left-wing Progressief Nederland has moved five seats clear in the polls while D66 slips to fourth behind Wilders' PVV.
body: Progressief Nederland (PRO) is now forecast to win around 26 seats with just under 17 percent of the vote, taking a five-seat lead. D66, which won 26 seats in November to become the largest party, has fallen to fourth.

The shift is driven by progressive voters unhappy with the course of Rob Jetten's minority coalition with the VVD and CDA. The PVV under Geert Wilders is projected at around 19 seats, edging D66 into fourth on roughly 18.

netherlands.summary: The VVD-CDA minority partnership is losing ground with the voters who put it in office.
body: The biggest movement in the polls since the general election has been progressive voters walking away from D66 in response to compromises made to hold the minority coalition together with the VVD and Christian democratic CDA.
With the campaign season warming up, the governing bloc faces pressure to show results on housing and cost of living before frustration hardens into a durable poll deficit.

netherlands.h3: Dutch growth stuck near 1 percent as inflation climbs
netherlands.summary: Forecasters see modest expansion this year with inflation picking up on higher energy prices.
body: Economic growth is projected to slow to about 1 percent in 2026 before firming to 1.4 percent in 2027. Spillovers from the Middle East conflict are weighing on activity through weaker consumption and soft external demand.
Inflation is expected to reach around 3.2 percent in 2026, driven largely by rising energy prices, a squeeze felt directly by households already stretched on housing costs.

netherlands.h3: Parties race to unblock housing supply
netherlands.summary: With the shortage still acute, Dutch parties are pushing reforms to speed construction and permitting.
body: The housing crisis remains a defining political issue, and parties across the spectrum are proposing ways to expedite construction and expand the housing stock. Streamlining land use and permitting is a common thread.
Economists argue that boosting supply, alongside longer-term market reforms, is the most durable way to ease affordability and support labour mobility across the country.

netherlands.h3: Student-senior housing scheme offers cheaper rooms
netherlands.summary: A programme pairing students with older residents is being pitched as one small answer to the shortage.
body: Among the housing initiatives drawing attention is a scheme that pairs students with seniors, offering rooms starting around 781.50 euros in the first year in exchange for companionship and light help.
Supporters frame it as a way to make better use of existing homes while easing loneliness, though it addresses only a sliver of a shortfall measured in hundreds of thousands of homes.

netherlands.h3: Middle East conflict feeds into Dutch energy bills
netherlands.summary: Higher energy costs tied to Gulf tensions are flowing through to Dutch consumers and industry.
body: The Netherlands' exposure to global trade makes it sensitive to the Middle East conflict, with higher energy prices weighing on private consumption and adding to the inflation picture.
For an economy already navigating tight housing and modest growth, elevated energy costs are an unwelcome drag heading into the autumn.

netherlands.h3: August opens hot, sunny and dry
netherlands.summary: The month began with tropical temperatures and little rain, and forecasters expect the drought to deepen.
body: Weather services said August would start hot and sunny across much of the country, with the south recording the year's fourth heatwave. Rain is scarce in the near-term outlook.
The combination of heat and dryness is straining farms, gardens and waterways, and keeping water conservation on the agenda for households and municipalities alike.

netherlands.h3: Rhine trade under pressure from low water
netherlands.summary: Shrinking river levels are complicating cargo movements that link Dutch ports to German industry.
body: Low water on the Rhine is forcing barges to carry lighter loads, raising freight costs on a corridor that ties Rotterdam and the Dutch waterway network to German manufacturing.
Repeated dry summers are turning what used to be rare disruptions into a recurring seasonal risk for the region's logistics.

netherlands.summary: The 2026-27 Dutch top flight begins on August 7, opening a new football season.
body: The VriendenLoterij Eredivisie, the 71st edition of the Dutch top division, is scheduled to run from August 7, 2026 to May 23, 2027. Clubs are wrapping up pre-season ahead of the opening weekend.
The new campaign brings the usual questions about whether the traditional powers can hold off ambitious challengers over a long domestic season.

mood.p: The Netherlands opens August in the grip of a fourth heatwave, tropical sun over the Randstad and temperatures pushing the low thirties in the south. The mood is summery but uneasy: the drought is deepening, inland peat dikes are drying out and river levels are falling fast enough to worry water managers and German barge trade alike. Politics is stirring too, with the campaign heating up as fast as the weather and Eredivisie football only days from kickoff.
